newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's BA/American decision seen before November.
newsitem.headline: EU's BA/American decision seen before November.

text.p: Any regulatory delays in dealing with the alliance between British Airways and AMR's American Airlines should no be imputed to the European Commission, EU sources said on Wednesday.
Reacting to comments by BA's chairman Robert Ayling that the deal may be called off if not cleared by November, a Commission spokesman said: "We won't take that long".
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said last week that the Commission's probe into the alliance would certainly go beyond its August summer break.

EU competition officials are expected to meet with their American counterparts this month, the sources said. They also said the Commission may take a final stance on the alliance before Britain announces its decision.

Ayling was quoted by the Financial Times on Wednesday as saying that BA wanted the deal approved by November, when take-off and landing slots will be allocated for the summer 1998 season. The comments were later confirmed by a company spokesman.

The alliance is being investigated by the Department of Transportation in the United States and by Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT). The Commission also started its own probe and must ensure any UK decision will respect EU rules banning abuse of dominant position and agreements restrictive of competition in the Union.

The Commission has informed the British authorities of its view that the deal would dominate flights between the U.S and London's congested Heathrow airport and that on 13 transatlantic routes it would eliminate competition altogether.

The EU sources appeared satisfied with a recent proposal by the U.S. General Accounting Office under which six U.S. airlines that do not currently serve Heathrow should obtain enough slots to operate 23 daily round-trip flights.
But they would not say whether the proposal reflected the Commission's own demands.

Any slots given to American airline rivals of BA and American were likely to benefit European companies as well because of the recent wave of transatlatic air alliances such as that between Lufthansa and United Airlines, on the one hand, and between Delta Air Lines, Swissair, Austrian Airlines and Sabena, on the other hand.

The OFT said in a preliminary ruling in December that it would clear the alliance on the condition the two airlines gave up 168 weekly take-off slots, enough for 12 daily round-trip flights. The announcement triggered an angry warning from Van Miert who said in a letter to British Trade Secretary Ian Lang that this was not enough and that the EU would challenge such decision in the European court if necessary.
EU and British antitrust authorities now appear to be cooperating closely on the issue to avoid conflicting rulings.
